title: Gated SDK request rubric: language gaps, auth patterns, and streaming ergonomics
creator: Diego Morales
description:
Summary:
We need a repeatable, lightweight rubric to gate and prioritize incoming SDK and client-library feature requests from enterprise customers. Requests hitting our intake range from small language bindings and auth nitpicks to streaming ergonomics that affect UX and latency. Without a common triage model, PMs and Eng spend cycles re-evaluating similar asks, and enterprise sales get inconsistent signals on delivery timelines.

Scope:
- Define criteria for evaluating language bindings (usage signal, integration cost, maintenance burden).
- Standardize auth patterns (token vs. delegated SSO flow vs. HMAC/KMS patterns) and when we accept provider-specific hooks.
- Establish streaming ergonomics checklist (backpressure, reconnect, chunked vs event messages, SDK helpers for resume).
- Produce clear outcomes: accept, backlog, prototype, or decline with rationale.
- Provide templated responses and required artifacts for acceptance (API contract examples, test harnesses, sample apps).

Background / motivation:
Multiple enterprise customers have raised similar asks in the last 6 months: one-off language bindings (Rust, Elixir), requests for a first-class delegated SSO flow in SDKs, and a few blockers caused by poor streaming reconnection behavior in our Node and Python clients. Feedback to date was handled ad-hoc. This has led to duplicated engineering proposals and unclear prioritization.

Proposed rubric (high level):
1) Customer signal (25%): number of unique customers, ARR/contract size, number of active users relying on the workflow.
2) Integration cost (25%): estimated eng effort (hours), infra change, maintenance surface (matrix of bindings/support).
3) Security/Compliance surface (20%): does the request touch encryption/KMS, audit logs, or introduce a data residency vector?
4) Product impact (20%): blocks go-to-market, reduces costs, or unlocks major feature adoption.
5) Developer ergonomics / time-to-value (10%): measured via pilot feedback or dev time saved.

Deliverables:
- One-page triage rubric doc with scoring explanation and examples (link: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SDK/pages/triage-rubric).
- Intake template for customer success and sales to populate (language, traffic patterns, security needs, example prompts).
- Sample SDK acceptance checklist (API surface, backpressure tests, auth demo app, integration smoke tests).
- Three prioritized candidate items (language binding: Rust stub; delegated SSO pattern; streaming reconnect helper) to pilot the rubric.

Trade-offs considered:
- Pursuing more language bindings increases community adoption but also multiplies maintenance. We recommend a staged approach: officially support a language only after an incubation period with automated CI and at least one production customer.
- Granting provider-specific auth hooks can accelerate adoption but complicates backward compatibility; prefer well-scoped extension points over ad-hoc provider flags.

Acceptance criteria:
- Triage rubric published and shared with Solutions & Sales (link above).
- Intake template adopted by CSMs and used in >=3 new SDK requests within 2 weeks.
- Pilot initiative approved for one language binding and one auth flow with scope and rough estimate.
- SDK team has a minimal streaming reconnect helper and unit tests merged behind a feature flag.

Metrics to measure success:
- Time-to-decision on SDK requests reduced from average 12 days to <=5 days.
- Reduction in duplicate eng proposals (measured via internal tag counts) by 50% in next quarter.
- Pilot customer satisfaction (NPS-style) >= 8/10 for implemented pilots.

Rollout plan:
Week 0-1: Draft rubric and intake template; gather PM/Eng/DS feedback.
Week 2: Finalize rubric; publish doc; training session for CS and Sales.
Week 3-6: Run pilots; collect metrics and iterate.
Week 7: Decide go/no-go for wider adoption and resource commits.

Notes on scope exclusions:
- This ticket does not commit to full language support for any language; pilots only.
- Does not include work to fully re-architect streaming protocol (that becomes a follow-up if pilot shows broad demand).
